pages.title: AI in litigation series: An update on AI copyright cases in 2026 | Global law firm | Norton Rose Fulbright
pages.raw_content:
AI in litigation series: An update on AI copyright cases in 2026 | Global law firm | Norton Rose Fulbright
Skip to main content
As
artificial intelligence
(AI) continues to expand its breadth of capabilities and scope of use, it continues to challenge existing legal principles in new and varied ways.
Copyright
issues are at the forefront of these challenges and have seen significant
litigation
related to the use of AI and ownership of the end products created.
In general, copyright law covers and protects “original works of authorship fixed in any tangible medium of expression.”
1
An original work of authorship is a work that is independently created by a human author and possesses at least some minimal degree of creativity. A work is “fixed” when it is captured, either by or under the authority of an author, in a sufficiently permanent medium such that the work can be perceived, reproduced or communicated for more than a short time. Simply put, copyright protects the
expression
, not the
idea
.
The
US Copyright Office
recognized AI’s potential disruption to copyright law years ago and in 2023 launched its official initiative on AI to examine AI’s impact to copyright law more closely. To that end, the US Copyright Office has released two reports on AI’s impact already, the second of which was focused on the “copyrightability” of material created with or while using AI. The report noted that, generally, “copyright protection in the United States requires human authorship. This foundational principle is based on the Copyright Clause in the Constitution and the language of the Copyright Act as interpreted by the courts. The Copyright Clause grants Congress the authority to “secur[e] for limited times to authors . . . the exclusive right to their . . . writings.” As the Supreme Court has explained, “the author [of a copyrighted work] is . . . the person who translates an idea into a fixed, tangible expression entitled to copyright protection.” No court has recognized copyright in material created by non-humans, and those that have spoken on this issue have rejected the possibility.
2
In the context of generative AI, in the US at least, copyright law does not currently protect AI outputs.
These principles have been tested recently, with numerous copyright infringement cases filed in the US against AI model providers and users. Many of these cases raise fundamental questions about whether training AI on copyrighted works constitutes fair use, whether AI-generated outputs infringe copyrights or are copyrightable and who bears liability for potentially infringing outputs. Some of these cases are still pending, while others have settled.
Here, we analyze six of the most notable AI-related copyright cases and discuss their effects on copyright law and AI usage. Namely, (1)
Thaler v. Perlmutte
r
3
; (2)
Thomson Reuters v. Ross Intelligence
;
4
(3)
Bartz et al. v. Anthropic
;
5
(4)
Kadrey et al. v. Meta Platforms Inc.
;
6
(5)
In Re OpenAI, Inc. Copyright Infringement Litigation
7
; and (6)
Disney et al. v. Midjourney
.
8
Summary of the cases
Thaler v. Perlmutter
: Dr. Thaler sued the US Copyright Office seeking judicial review of its refusal to register his AI-generated artwork. On March 2, 2026, the Supreme Court denied certiorari of Dr. Stephen Thaler’s appeal of the lower court’s decision granting summary judgment in favor of the US Copyright Office (and thus upholding the US Copyright Office’s refusal to issue a copyright), confirming the principle that material must still have human authorship to be copyrightable.
Thomson Reuters v. Ross Intelligence
: Thomson Reuters sued an AI-driven competitor for use of its Westlaw headnotes and key numbers in training its own platform. Importantly, Ross Intelligence’s platform is not a
generative
AI model, but rather an AI-driven case search tool. The court granted summary judgment in favor of Thomson Reuters, finding that the headnotes were original and protected and that Ross Intelligence's use of the headnotes to train its AI legal research tool was not fair use. The case is currently on appeal before the Third Circuit.
Bartz et al. v. Anthropic
: A group of authors sued Anthropic in a class action lawsuit, alleging that Anthropic illegally copied their books. After significant briefing, the court ruled that AI training on copyrighted books constitutes fair use, but storing pirated copies does not. After that ruling, the case settled for US$1.5 billion, with an estimated payout of approximately US$3,000 per work.
Kadrey et al. v. Meta Platforms Inc
.: Similar to
Bartz
, the plaintiffs here sued Meta alleging that it committed copyright infringement when training its Llama large language model (LLM) on the plaintiffs’ books. The court granted a partial motion to dismiss on fair use grounds as for training the LLM. Claims related to alleged reproduction of pirated works during “seeding” in the torrenting process remain active in the Northern District of California.
In Re OpenAI, Inc., Copyright Infringement Litigation
:
9
The plaintiffs sued OpenAI and another defendant, alleging that they infringed Plaintiffs’ copyrights by using their works to train LLMs and by generating unauthorized, infringing outputs through ChatGPT. They further contend that ChatGPT relied on these training datasets to produce detailed summaries and outlines of their copyrighted books. The MDL is currently pending before the Southern District of New York.
Disney et al. v. Midjourney
: Several major
entertainment
companies sued Midjourney for allegedly, and unlawfully, copying copyrighted works to train its AI image-generation model and that the model reproduces derivative images of their copyrighted characters. The case is currently pending before the Central District of California.
Thaler v. Perlmutter
Dr. Stephen Thaler, a computer scientist, developed a generative AI system called the "Creativity Machine.” This system created an artwork titled “A Recent Entrance to Paradise,” shown below:
10
In 2018, Dr. Thaler filed a copyright application with the US Copyright Office for the artwork. On the application, he identified the Creativity Machine as the sole author and himself as the owner, acknowledging that the work lacks traditional human authorship. The Copyright Office denied the registration, relying on its longstanding human authorship requirement under the Copyright Act.
Dr. Thaler then sought judicial review in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia, arguing the Copyright Office’s decision was wrong on constitutional, statutory and policy grounds and asserting ownership under the work-for-hire doctrine. Both parties moved for summary judgment. Judge Beryl Howell granted summary judgment in favor of the Copyright Office, holding that human authorship is a “bedrock requirement of copyright.”
11
The court also held that Dr. Thaler could not rely on the work-for-hire statute because that provision “presuppose[s] that an interest exists to be claimed.”
12
The “image autonomously generated” by the Creativity Machine was not such an interest because it “was never eligible for copyright,” so there was no copyright to transfer to Dr. Thaler even if he were the Creativity Machine’s employer.
13
Finally, the court found that Dr. Thaler waived his argument that he should own the copyright because he created and used the Creativity Machine. Dr. Thaler subsequently appealed to the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit. On March 18, 2025, the panel affirmed Judge Howell’s ruling. The court explained that although the Copyright Act does not explicitly define “author,” multiple provisions make clear that authors must be human. The court further noted that Congress adopted the Copyright Office’s human authorship requirement when enacting the Copyright Act. The panel also rejected Dr. Thaler’s alternative arguments based on the work-for-hire doctrine, reasoning that this provision requires the underlying work to be eligible for copyright protection in the first instance. Finally, the court found that Dr. Thaler had waived his argument that he should be recognized as the author by virtue of creating the AI platform, as he failed to raise this claim during administrative proceedings.
On October 9, 2025, Dr. Thaler petitioned for a writ of certiorari to the United States Supreme Court, arguing that the lower courts’ decisions have created a “chilling effect on anyone else considering using AI creatively.”
14
In response, the Solicitor General, on behalf of the Copyright Office, contended that Dr. Thaler had consistently disclaimed any human contributions to the work and thus the work should not be copyrightable. The US Supreme Court denied certiorari on March 2, 2026, thereby reaffirming human authorship as a foundational requirement of US copyright law, even in this era of rapid AI advancement.
To be clear, this case does not necessarily prohibit copyright protection for works created with AI
assistance
; human contributions with AI assistive use may be protectable. Here, Dr. Thaler explicitly and repeatedly disclaimed any human creative input, so the court did not address how much human involvement is necessary to support copyright registration for AI-assisted works. That issue is still ripe for resolution.
Thomson Reuters v. Ross Intelligence
Thomson Reuters Enterprise Centre GmbH sued Ross Intelligence Inc. in Delaware, alleging that Ross Intelligence—via a vendor—infringed Thomson Reuters' copyrights in its Westlaw headnotes and by actually copying and using them to train its competing AI-powered legal research tool.
In late 2023, the court denied cross summary judgment motions in this case. But as the case was progressing to trial, the court invited the parties to resubmit those motions. On February 11, 2025, the court granted partial summary judgment in favor of Thomson Reuters, finding that (1) Thomson Reuters’ Westlaw's headnotes and Key Number System were original and protected by copyright, and (2) Ross Intelligence's actual copying of the headnotes was not fair use. Specifically, its vendor was contracted to create training data in the form of “Bulk Memos,” which were compilations of legal questions created by lawyers with good and bad answers to help train the platform. Its vendor created these Bulk Memos using Westlaw headnotes. To reach its decision, the court reviewed the thousands of Bulk Memos at issue and compared them against the headnotes and the underlying case opinions; after doing so, the court concluded that the headnotes are sufficiently original, and that Ross did copy them.
In fact, the court found that the 2,243 headnotes at issue matched content so closely that "no reasonable jury could find otherwise"
15
that actual copying occurred. Ross's defenses of innocent infringement, merger, scènes à faire and copyright misuse were all rejected. As for the Key Number System, the court indicated it was not clear if or how those were used, and so actual copying on those was left to the jury to decide.
When the court analyzed the four fair use factors, it found that Ross's use was commercial and not transformative because it created a competitive tool with the same function as Westlaw. Critically, the court emphasized that Ross's tool is not generative AI, finding that it does not write legal research memos or opinions and that it is merely a search tool that identifies cases in response to the user's legal research questions. The factors regarding the nature of the work and the amount used weighed in Ross's favor, given the narrow scope of protection afforded the headnotes and the fact that they did not appear to Ross’s end users. However, the effect on the market heavily favored Thomson Reuters, as Ross's tool was directly competitive and undercut Westlaw's market.
On May 23, 2025, the court granted Ross Intelligence's motion for interlocutory appeal and stay pending appeal, noting that "the questions here are hard."
16
In its appeal brief filed in September 2025, Ross Intelligence argued that if the decision stands, it will have "sweeping consequences for innovation"
17
in both legal research and artificial intelligence. The issues on appeal include whether headnotes and Key Numbers are copyrightable and whether Ross Intelligence’s use was fair. That appeal is still pending.
Bartz et al. v. Anthropic
This class action, which ultimately included nearly half a million authors, was filed in August 2024 by authors Andrea Bartz, Charles Graeber and Kirk Wallace Johnson against Anthropic. The authors challenged Anthropic's use of their books (both lawfully acquired and pirated) to train its Claude LLM and to keep in its “central library” for undisclosed future purposes. The plaintiffs alleged that Anthropic illegally downloaded over seven million copyrighted books from "shadow libraries" like LibGen, and then ultimately changed course and acquired the books legally. Notably, the claims did not assert that Claude’s outputs were infringing; the case’s focus was on training and retention in the “central library.”
On June 23, 2025, the court found that Anthropic’s training was fair use, but that storing pirated copies was not. The decision stopped short of explicitly addressing whether training conducted with pirated source copies is fair use. However, the court expressed skepticism that "any subsequent fair use” could ever justify pirated downloads.
18
This skepticism suggests a doctrinal tension: while the fair‑use holding did not depend on lawful acquisition, the decision intimates that obtaining copies from piracy sites may erode the defense, even in a training context.
The court’s fair use analysis concluded that training data was ”transformative—spectacularly so.”
19
and “among the most transformative many of us will see in our lifetimes.”
20
Training an LLM involves feeding it billions of words or “tokens,” and the model converts those tokens into numbers, then repeatedly adjusts its internal parameters, known as weights, so it gets better and better at predicting the next token. The more material and the higher quality of material used to train the LLM, the better it will learn language and be able to generate content and complete tasks. The court likened this training process to reading books to learn human language: "To make anyone pay specifically for the use of a book each time they read it, each time they recall it from memory, each time they later draw upon it when writing new things in new ways would be unthinkable."
21
Because the works at issue here were novels and other long-form books, the court found that the second factor looking at the nature of the works favored the authors. However, that factor is typically given little weight. The court also concluded that copying entire works was "reasonably necessary" to train an LLM. Critically, the court also found that since the training data is never shown to users and doesn't replace the market for the original books, the market-effect factor favored Anthropic. In the court’s view, the fourth fair use factor protects against
replacement
, not competition. It was critical to the court’s decision that the plaintiffs did not allege that Claude would replicate significant amounts of text that it was trained on, and Anthropic had incorporated safeguards to prevent this from happening. The court also noted that authors are not entitled to licensing revenue for training
because
it is a fair use, and that a market for licensing training data is not one the Copyright Act entitles authors to exploit.
However, the court went on to find that Anthropic's acquisition and storage of over seven million pirated books was not protected by fair use, as obtaining and storing pirated books was not necessary to train the LLM. Further, Anthropic's subsequent decision not to train Claude on pirated copies did not absolve its liability for storing the works in the first place. There was no “get out of jail free” card for downloading pirated copies simply because the intended end use might be transformative.
The case later settled for a total of US$1.5 billion. The settlement terms include the destruction of Anthropic's pirated dataset and are limited to past use of training data, not outputs. Based on this value, authors in the class are estimated to receive a payout of approximately US$3,000 per work before fees and costs. The class's attorneys have requested US$300 million (20 percent) in fees and US$2 million in expenses.
The settlement halted a trial that might have tested the boundaries of copyright statutory damages. Because statutory copyright damages can reach US$150,000 per infringed work, Anthropic’s exposure theoretically extended into the hundreds of billions of dollars, raising existential risk for the company. The effects will likely resonate well beyond a single suit. In fact, another group of plaintiffs—music publishers—subsequently moved to amend their complaint against Anthropic to add piracy claims similar to what the plaintiffs alleged here. We may see other AI platforms settle with creators as cases get closer to trial to avoid potentially astronomical damages.
Kadrey et al. v. Meta Platforms Inc.
In this case, filed in 2023, the plaintiffs (another group of authors including Richard Kadrey, Sarah Silverman and Junot Diaz) alleged that Meta infringed the authors' copyrights by training its AI LLM (Llama) models on their books. This suit also includes allegations that the books were pirated from “shadow libraries.” Importantly, in this suit, the allegations specifically include that Meta downloaded the books via torrenting.
Similar to the
Bartz
court, on June 25, 2025, this court granted partial dismissal in Meta’s favor on the basis of fair use, finding that the training was transformative. However, the court differed from the
Bartz
court’s opinion on the fourth fair-use factor—market harm—criticizing the plaintiffs’ "half-hearted" arguments of market harm.
22
It also diverged from the
Bartz
court in how it treated training the model on pirated works, squarely holding that LLM training constitutes fair use regardless of whether the underlying materials were obtained from legitimate sources or not.
In a separate opinion, the court ruled in favor of Meta on the plaintiffs’ Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) claims regarding the removal of copyright management information (CMI) in training Llama. The DMCA prohibits removal of CMI that will “induce, enable, facilitate, or conceal an infringement of any right under this title.” The court found that because the training was fair use, the removal of the information was not in furtherance of any infringement and so the DMCA claim fails.
The court had some strong criticisms in this opinion. Not only did the court call out the plaintiffs for failing—in the court’s view—to put forth any good arguments about the fourth fair use factor, but the court also explicitly disagreed with the
Bartz
court’s analysis on this factor, which this court considered to be the most important factor in the analysis. Of the plaintiffs’ arguments, the court wrote:
This . . . ruling only affects the rights of these thirteen authors—not the countless others whose works Meta used to train its models. And, as should now be clear, this ruling does not stand for the proposition that Meta’s use of copyrighted materials to train its language models is lawful. It stands only for the proposition that these plaintiffs made the wrong arguments and failed to develop a record in support of the right one.
23
To summarize, the authors focused their market harm arguments on two theories: either that the model could create substantially similar outputs to their books, or that Meta would usurp the market for licensing training materials. The court found both arguments unpersuasive. Llama is safeguarded against regurgitating the training materials and there was no evidence it had done so here. Similarly, regarding the potential market for licensing, the court found that this argument was circular. If harm from the loss of fees paid to license a work for a transformative purpose is actionable, the plaintiff would win every time.
However, the court did identify what it considered to be a potentially more persuasive argument: that AI models can flood the market with similar texts and stifle competition. In the court’s view, that could be exactly the sort of market harm the fair use analysis seeks to prevent. The court emphasized that the fact that books like the plaintiffs’ here make for better training data supports this argument; in essence, that training the LLM on books can make it better at diluting the market for those books. However, the court found that the plaintiffs here did not build any record to support this argument, so the court found in Meta’s favor.
There are still some claims that survived summary judgment. Specifically, there is a question of whether, during the torrenting process, Meta “seeded” the books, essentially meaning it may have distributed the pirated copies to third parties. On December 11, 2025, the authors moved to amend their lawsuit to add a contributory infringement claim related to this issue. The authors claim they "were in the dark about how Meta obtained plaintiffs' copyrighted works" and that their understanding of Meta's alleged "torrenting activities" has only recently "crystallized."
24
They allege that new log data suggested that Meta engaged in large-scale torrenting, which prompted the authors to refine their class definition before discovery. Meta has opposed the plaintiffs’ motion and the parties have been engaged in cross-briefing as recently as last week. The parties’ latest arguments center on whether Meta belatedly asserted a new fair use defense regarding the “seeding” process and whether schedule adjustments and further discovery are needed.
In short, the case is far from closed on fair use for training data and demonstrates that courts—even those sitting in the same district—can reach different conclusions when confronted with similar facts. This will be an interesting case to monitor, and we might see other authors using the court’s decision here as a blueprint in their own complaints regarding the market harm factor. The fact that courts are splitting on this issue may also encourage the appellate courts to weigh in on whether training generative AI models on pirated works can ever be fair use.
In Re OpenAI, Inc. copyright infringement litigation
In April 2025, the United States Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation consolidated twelve cases against OpenAI and another defendant originating in the Southern District of New York and the Northern District of California. The MDL encompasses class actions originally filed in California by authors, New York suits brought by news organizations, DMCA-focused suits and a case brought by an online video creator. The panel found that these cases involve common questions of fact regarding the defendants' use of copyrighted works, without consent or compensation, to train their LLMs. The consolidated matter was assigned to the Southern District of New York and aims to streamline the infringement claims against OpenAI and provide some consistency in rulings.
In the MDL, the plaintiffs allege that the defendants infringed their copyrights by downloading and reproducing their works to train OpenAI's LLMs and to create infringing outputs through OpenAI's ChatGPT. The plaintiffs further claim that ChatGPT used these training datasets to generate comprehensive summaries and outlines of their copyrighted books, which they contend constitutes infringement. OpenAI generally denies the claims but admitted to several factual allegations concerning the datasets used to train its GPT‑2 and GPT‑3 models. OpenAI asserted numerous affirmative defenses, including failure to state a claim under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6), fair use, de minimis copying, invalid or nonexistent copyright ownership, and lack of provable injury. In its motion to dismiss, filed on July 14, 2025, OpenAI argued that the court cannot assess whether ChatGPT’s outputs are substantially similar to plaintiffs’ works because the consolidated complaint neither cites nor attaches examples of the allegedly infringing outputs. OpenAI also claimed that the outputs at issue are similar to the news‑article summaries that the court held were not substantially similar to copyrighted works in related litigations.
In an opinion dated October 27, 2025, the court held that “[i]t is sufficient to defeat OpenAI's motion to dismiss that plaintiffs have alleged some outputs that a reasonable jury could find are substantially similar to plaintiffs’ works.”
25
Further, the court noted that nothing in its opinion “is intended to suggest a view on whether the allegedly infringing outputs are protected as fair uses of the original works.”
26
Most recently, on January 5, 2026, the court ordered OpenAI to produce all 20 million output logs noting that “OpenAI identifies no caselaw requiring a court to order the least burdensome discovery possible or to explain specifically why it rejects a party's discovery proposal.”
27
And just earlier this week, on March 9, 2026, the Court granted the plaintiffs’ motion to compel and ordered OpenAI to produce “the reservoirs of 78 million and 10 million logs,” on top of the 20 million log sample that was already ordered to be produced.
28
Discovery is ongoing.
Disney et al. v. Midjourney
In this case, Disney and its subsidiaries, including Lucasfilm and Marvel, along with other studios, allege that Midjourney unlawfully copied their copyrighted works to train its AI image-generation service, and that it continues to infringe because it continues to reproduce, publicly display and distribute derivative images of the companies’ iconic characters. Below are some of the images generated by Midjourney highlighted in the plaintiffs' complaint:
The plaintiffs assert that Midjourney engaged in willful misconduct by ignoring cease-and-desist demands, failing to implement copyright safeguards and actively promoting infringing outputs as a feature to attract subscribers, thereby generating hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue. Accordingly, the plaintiffs seek injunctive relief, statutory or actual damages (up to US$150,000 per work for willful infringement), disgorgement of profits and attorneys' fees.
Notably, in a related development, Disney and OpenAI recently signed a deal allowing OpenAI's Sora to generate AI videos featuring Disney's iconic characters. Under the three-year deal, Sora can create short, user-prompted videos featuring over 200 characters from Disney’s most beloved franchises, along with costumes, props, vehicles and themed environments. As part of the agreement, Disney will invest US$1 billion in OpenAI and become a major customer, leveraging AI for new products and Disney+ experiences. Both companies pledged to uphold user safety and creator rights, with Disney emphasizing its goal of extending storytelling through generative AI while respecting and protecting creators and their works.
This development may spark a trend toward formal licensing of copyrighted material for generative AI use. Agreements like this may also have an impact on the fair use analysis as well. Licensing agreements of this nature could materially impact the fourth, market-harm factor by providing evidence of an active, remunerative licensing market for generative AI use. Put another way, big licensing deals like this one give concrete evidence of the potential market for creators and copyright holders to exploit their content in connection with training and AI content outputs. Unlicensed AI uses are more likely to be viewed as impairing a protected market, which could weigh against fair use.
Summary of trends in AI-related copyright cases
Several key patterns and trends emerge from these AI-related copyright cases:
First, courts are grappling with fundamental questions about AI and copyright, including: (1) whether copyrighted works can be used to train AI models under fair use, and whether that answer depends on if the works were acquired legitimately or pirated; (2) whether AI-generated outputs constitute fair use or infringement; and (3) who owns and can copyright AI-generated or AI-assisted content.
Second, the fair use analysis in AI training cases is evolving, and different courts may reach varied conclusions. This revolutionary
technology
presents many issues of first impression, requiring courts to apply the law in new ways. For instance, the
Ross
court emphasized that Ross Intelligence's tool was not generative AI but a search tool, distinguishing its analysis from cases involving generative models. Even among generative AI cases, courts have diverged. The
Bartz
court found that AI training was fair use, but expressed skepticism that "any subsequent fair use" could justify pirated downloads.
29
In contrast, the
Kadrey
court squarely held that LLM training constitutes fair use regardless of whether the underlying materials were obtained from legitimate sources. The judges also differed on the market harm factor. The
Kadrey
court left the door open for a different outcome in other LLM training cases based on market harm, in stark contrast to the
Bartz
court’s view on fair use. This emphasizes the fact that courts are reaching different conclusions when presented with similar claims and facts.
Third, courts have consistently found that the source of training data is significant. Courts may permit AI companies to train on copyrighted works if they obtained those works lawfully, as demonstrated by the
Bartz
court. However, as
Bartz
and
Kadrey
show, the retention and/or distribution of pirated copies can create separate liability independent of training.
Fourth, licensing is accelerating and emerging as a potential solution to these issues. The Disney-OpenAI agreement shows a trend towards formal licensing of copyrighted material for generative AI use, setting the stage for how entertainment companies monetize IP in AI-driven platforms. Such arrangements may become the industry standard for using copyrighted content in AI training in order to avoid costly and uncertain litigation.
Fifth, liability for outputs remains on the table. Cases such as
Disney
will test responsibility for infringing or look-alike AI outputs and marketing uses. The question of whether outputs infringe may depend on whether they reproduce protected expression or merely reflect learned patterns.
Conclusion: Practical takeaways
More and more companies are rapidly investing in, using and planning to grow their use of GenAI. Given the widespread deployment of, and significant volume of information generated by, these tools, new litigation and claims will quickly arise as well. Companies seeking to utilize AI tools in a way that would impact their ability to protect materials under copyright laws should consider the following practical takeaways from these cases:
First, understand how the tools that are considered to be used will actually be used and ensure that before the company brings the same in for use that it conducts due diligence on AI tools and their training data sources, reviewing license rights and terms of service and assessing potential exposure from using AI-generated content.
Second, be proactive by implementing monitoring systems for AI-generated content, communicating clear policies regarding AI use, scanning outputs for potential infringement issues and training employees on copyright considerations when using AI tools.
Third, stay informed on all legal developments including related case law which generally moves quicker than regulation as courts continue to refine the application of fair use doctrine to AI training and outputs. The pending appeals in
Thomson Reuters
and ongoing litigation in other cases may significantly shape the legal landscape.
Fourth, consider licensing arrangements where appropriate, as the trend toward formal licensing agreements between content owners and AI companies may reduce litigation risk and provide clearer rights to use copyrighted materials.
Our team has significant experience counseling clients on mitigation of risks associated with training and deploying AI models, and in general dealing with AI from both a governance and a litigation perspective. For any questions regarding issues relating to AI and
intellectual property
matters, please contact us.

Artificial Intelligence: Latest Government Regulations and Copyright Litigation Updates - Foster Garvey

Legal Alerts
Artificial Intelligence: Latest Government Regulations and Copyright Litigation Updates
09.18.25
04.30.26
Download PDF
By: Landon Coles (2025 Summer Associate),
Joshua A. Bloomgarden
,
Hillary Hughes
Artificial intelligence (“
AI
”) continues to grow as a fixture of daily life, but not everyone is embracing it (according to a recent
Pew Research Center survey
, about half of U.S. adults (51%) say they are
more
concerned than excited
about the increased use of AI), and even fewer have an understanding of how to leverage this technology while respecting creators’ intellectual property rights. Through a patchwork of government regulations and ongoing litigation, we are gradually beginning to see contours emerge around AI policy, albeit with plenty of grey areas persisting.
Government Regulation
Comprehensive federal regulation, specifically regarding copyright infringement, continues to remain elusive. Legislation has largely been aimed at addressing specific harms caused by AI technology, such as deepfake technology to spread misinformation on elections and candidates, generate nonconsensual pornography or to mimic music artists’ voices without permission.
President Donald J. Trump has taken an expansive approach to AI, signing an Executive Order in January 2025 to revoke “existing AI policies and directives that act as barriers to American AI innovation,” though the application of that Executive Order is unclear. In May 2025, President Trump signed into law the bipartisan
Take It Down Act
which makes it illegal to “knowingly publish” or threaten to publish intimate images without a person’s consent, including AI-created “deepfakes.”
In response to the void of federal regulation, states have enacted a patchwork of legislation with over 30 states enacting laws addressing deepfakes as of May 2025.
Litigation Related to AI Copyright Infringement
On the copyright front, leading technology companies such Meta, ChatGPT-maker OpenAI and Microsoft have been embroiled in controversy in recent years related to the practice of training AI language models on copyrighted material. These companies have argued they are immune from liability under the “fair use” doctrine, pursuant to which courts apply a four-factor test on the allegedly infringing uses analyzing: (1) the purpose and character of the use, (2) the nature of the copyrighted work, (3) the amount and substantiality of the portion used and (4) the effect of the use on the potential market.
Bartz v. Anthropic PBC
In
Bartz v. Anthropic PBC
, the United States District Court for the Northern District of California ruled in favor of Anthropic, finding that use of copyrighted books to train large language models is a fair use due to its “highly transformative” nature.
Bartz v. PBC
, 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 136877, *56
. There, the court distinguished Anthropic’s conversion of purchased print books to digital format for a central library (which the court found to be a fair use), as opposed to Anthropic’s use of pirated copies of books (which the court found not to be a fair use). Anthropic has since reached a landmark $1.5 billion settlement (pending court approval) with the authors and copyright holders of the pirated works.
Kadrey v. Meta Platforms, Inc.
In a later case, the United States District Court for the Northern District of California, ruled in favor of Meta, finding that the company’s use of the plaintiffs’ copyrighted books to train its large language model Llama, was highly transformative and favored fair use under the first fair use factor.
Kadrey v. Meta Platforms, Inc.
, 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 121064, *1
The court did limit the scope of the ruling, stating the case is “not a class action,” and “does not stand for the proposition that Meta’s use of copyrighted materials to train its language models is lawful.”
Thomson Reuters Enterprise Centre GMBH v. Ross Intelligence Inc.
Earlier this year, Thomson Reuters sued Ross Intelligence, alleging that Ross violated Thomson Reuters’ copyright in instances where Ross used Thomson Reuters’ Westlaw headnotes to train Ross’ new AI legal-research search engine. The United States District Court for Delaware granted partial summary judgement for Thomson Reuters, affirming that Ross improperly used 2,243 Westlaw headnotes and that Ross’s use harmed the market for Thomson Reuters’s headnotes and derivative products.
Thomson Reuters Enter. Ctr. GmbH v. Ross Intel. Inc.
, 765 F. Supp. 3d 382, 390 (D. Del. 2025)
Pending Cases
Earlier this year, several major publishers, including Conde Nast, The Atlantic, Politico and Vox sued AI startup, Cohere, alleging the improper use of more than 4,000 copyrighted works to train its large language model and unauthorized publishing of large portions of or entire articles for users while bypassing visits to the publishers’ websites.
In October 2024, Concord Music Group alongside several music publishers filed a copyright lawsuit against AI developer, Anthropic PBC, over its use of copyrighted song lyrics to train its AI model, Claude. In January 2025, the court entered a judgement permitting Anthropic to continue training its AI model while the litigation proceeded. As of July 2025, the case remains active, as the court will have to resolve the action, which seeks to enjoin Anthropic’s alleged use of unauthorized copies of the publishers’ song lyrics to train AI models.
A group of authors, including Sarah Silverman, filed suit over the unauthorized use of their novels by Anthropic to train its artificial intelligence chatbot, ChatGPT. Most of the claims, including claims for negligence, unjust enrichment and vicarious copyright infringement, have since been dismissed. The primary claim for direct copyright infringement remains pending.
Getty Images (US) alleged that Stability AI unlawfully used over 12 million Getty Images to train its Stable Diffusion model without consent. The case, currently before the UK High Court, saw Getty recently drop its direct copyright claims, choosing instead to focus on claims related to trademark, passing off and secondary infringement. A verdict on this case is expected later this year.
Please note that these cases are just a small survey of the many ongoing disputes between AI developers and copyrights holders, and the outcome of particular cases may vary based on the facts and technology at issue. As navigating intellectual property law in the age of AI continues to be a difficult task, Foster Garvey is actively monitoring these developments and we encourage you to contact us if you are in need of guidance.

Artificial intelligence and copyright - Wikipedia
Jump to content
From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Copyright law in the use of AI
In the 2020s, the
rapid advancement
of
deep learning
-based
generative artificial intelligence
models raised questions about the copyright status of AI-generated works, and about whether
copyright infringement
occurs when such are trained or used. This includes
text-to-image models
such as
Stable Diffusion
and
large language models
such as
GPT
. Large language models are trained on all the data which can be
scraped
from the Internet, often utilizing copyrighted material.
[
1
]
As of 2023, there were several pending U.S. lawsuits challenging the use of copyrighted data to train AI models, with defendants arguing that this falls under
fair use
.
[
2
]
Copyright status of AI-generated works
[
edit
]
The United States Copyright Office has declared that works not created by a human author, like
this "selfie" portrait taken by a monkey
, are not eligible for copyright protection.
Since most legal jurisdictions only grant copyright to original works of authorship by human authors, the definition of
originality
is central to the copyright status of AI-generated works.
[
3
]
United States
[
edit
]
The
Copyright Clause
states:
The Congress shall have the power ... To promote the Progress of .... useful Arts, by securing for limited Times to Authors ... the exclusive Right to their respective Writings...
The
US Congress
and Federal Courts have interpreted this clause as being limited to works "created by a human being",
[
4
]
declining to grant copyright to works generated without human intervention.
[
5
]
Some legal professionals have suggested that
Naruto v. Slater
(2018), in which the
U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals
held that
non-humans
cannot be copyright holders of
artistic works
, could be a potential precedent in copyright litigation over works created by generative AI.
[
6
]
Some have suggested that certain AI generations might be copyrightable in the U.S. and similar jurisdictions if it can be shown that the human who ran the AI program exercised sufficient originality in selecting the inputs to the AI or editing the AI's output.
[
5
]
[
4
]
Proponents of this view suggest that an AI model may be viewed as merely a tool (akin to a pen or a camera) used by its human operator to express their creative vision.
[
4
]
[
7
]
For example, proponents argue that if the standard of originality can be satisfied by an artist clicking the shutter button on a camera, then perhaps artists using generative AI should get similar deference, especially if they go through multiple rounds of revision to refine their prompts to the AI.
[
8
]
Other proponents argue that the Copyright Office is not taking a technology neutral approach to the use of AI or
algorithmic
tools. For other creative expressions (music, photography, writing) the test is effectively whether there is
de minimis
,
or limited human creativity. For works using AI tools, the Copyright Office has made the test a different one i.e. whether there is no more than
de minimis
technological involvement.
[
9
]
Théâtre D'opéra Spatial
, 2022, created using
Midjourney
, prompted by Jason M. Allen
This difference in approach can be seen in the recent decision in respect of a registration claim by Jason Matthew Allen for his work
Théâtre D'opéra Spatial
created using Midjourney and an upscaling tool. The Copyright Office stated:
The Board finds that the Work contains more than a de minimis amount of content generated by artificial intelligence ("AI"), and this content must therefore be disclaimed in an application for registration. Because Mr. Allen is unwilling to disclaim the AI-generated material, the Work cannot be registered as submitted.
[
10
]
As AI is increasingly used to generate literature, music, and other forms of art, the U.S. Copyright Office has released new guidance emphasizing whether works, including materials generated by artificial intelligence, exhibit a 'mechanical reproduction' nature or are the 'manifestation of the author's own creative conception'.
[
11
]
The U.S. Copyright Office published a Rule in March 2023 on a range of issues related to the use of AI, where they stated:
...because the Office receives roughly half a million applications for registration each year, it sees new trends in registration activity that may require modifying or expanding the information required to be disclosed on an application.
One such recent development is the use of sophisticated artificial intelligence ("AI") technologies capable of producing expressive material. These technologies "train" on vast quantities of preexisting human-authored works and use inferences from that training to generate new content. Some systems operate in response to a user's textual instruction, called a "prompt."
The resulting output may be textual, visual, or audio, and is determined by the AI based on its design and the material it has been trained on. These technologies, often described as "generative AI," raise questions about whether the material they produce is protected by copyright, whether works consisting of both human-authored and AI-generated material may be registered, and what information should be provided to the Office by applicants seeking to register them.
[
12
]
The Copyright Office further clarified in January 2025 that AI-assisted works where the creative expression of the human remains evident in the work can be copyrighted, which can include creative adaption of prompts for AI generators or usage of AI to assist in the creation process of a work, such as in
filmmaking
.
[
13
]
Works "where the expressive elements are determined by a machine" still remain uncopyrightable.
[
14
]
Following this guidance, the Copyright Office registered "A Single Piece of American Cheese", the first visual artwork composed solely of AI generated outputs as a composite work in January 2025.
[
15
]
The basis for the copyright involved arguing that human-driven selection, arrangement, and coordination involved in the creative process on a single work constituted sufficient human authorship to merit the copyright.
Both the federal and circuit courts in the District of Columbia have upheld the Copyright Office's refusal to register copyrights for works generated solely by machines, establishing that machine ownership would conflict with heritable property rights as establish by the Copyright Act of 1975.
[
16
]
As of March 2026
[
update
]
, the Supreme Court of the United States has denied hearing challenges to the Copyright Office's decision.
[
17
]
The
U.S. Patent and Trademark Office
(USPTO) similarly codified restrictions on the
patentability
of patents credits solely to AI authors in February 2024, following an August 2023 ruling in the case
Thaler v. Perlmutter
. In this case, the Patent Office denied grant to patents created by Stephen Thaler's AI program,
DABUS
due to the lack of a "natural person" on the patents' list of inventors. The
U.S. Court of Appeals
for the Federal Circuit upheld this decision.
[
18
]
[
19
]
In the subsequent rule-making, the USPTO allows for human inventors to incorporate the output of artificial intelligence, as long as this method is appropriately documented in the patent application.
[
20
]
However, it may become virtually impossible as when the inner workings and the use of AI in inventive transactions are not adequately understood or are largely unknown.
[
19
]
Representative
Adam Schiff
proposed the
Generative AI Copyright Disclosure Act
in April 2024. If passed, the bill would require AI companies to submit copyrighted works to the
Register of Copyrights
before releasing new generative AI systems. These companies would have to file these documents 30 days before publicly showing their AI tools.
[
21
]
United Kingdom
[
edit
]
Main article:
Copyright and artificial intelligence in the United Kingdom
Other jurisdictions include explicit statutory language related to computer-generated works, including the United Kingdom's
Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988
, which states:
In the case of a literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work which is computer-generated, the author shall be taken to be the person by whom the arrangements necessary for the creation of the work are undertaken.
[
7
]
However, the computer generated work law under UK law relates to autonomous creations by computer programs. Individuals using AI tools will usually be the authors of the works assuming they meet the minimum requirements for copyright work. The language used for computer generated work relates, in respect of AI, to the ability of the human programmers to have copyright in the autonomous productions of the AI tools (i.e. where there is no direct human input):
In so far as each composite frame is a computer generated work then the arrangements necessary for the creation of the work were undertaken by Mr Jones because he devised the appearance of the various elements of the game and the rules and logic by which each frame is generated and he wrote the relevant computer program. In these circumstances I am satisfied that Mr Jones is the person by whom the arrangements necessary for the creation of the works were undertaken and therefore is deemed to be the author by virtue of s.9(3)
[
22
]
The UK government has consulted on the use of generative tools and AI in respect of intellectual property leading to a proposed specialist Code of Practice:
[
23
]
"to provide guidance to support AI firms to access copyrighted work as an input to their models, whilst ensuring there are protections on generated output to support right holders of copyrighted work".
[
24
]
In October, 2023, The U.S. Copyright Office published a
notice of inquiry
and request for comments following its 2023 Registration Guidance.
[
25
]
China
[
edit
]
On November 27, 2023, the
Beijing
Internet Court issued a decision recognizing copyright in AI-generated images in a litigation.
[
26
]
As noted by a lawyer and AI art creator, the challenge for intellectual property regulators, legislators and the courts is how to protect human creativity in a technologically neutral fashion whilst considering the risks of automated AI factories. AI tools have the ability to autonomously create a range of material that is potentially subject to copyright (music, blogs, poetry, images, and technical papers) or other intellectual property rights (patents and design rights).
[
9
]
Training AI with copyrighted data
[
edit
]
Deep learning models
source
large data sets from the Internet such as publicly available images and the text of web pages. The text and images are then converted into
numeric formats
the AI can analyze. A deep learning model identifies patterns linking the encoded text and image data and learns which text concepts correspond to elements in images. Through repetitive testing, the model refines its accuracy by matching images to text descriptions. The trained model undergoes validation to evaluate its skill in generating or manipulating new images using only the text prompts provided after the training process.
[
27
]
When assembling these
training datasets
involves making copies of copyrighted works, this has raised the question of whether this process infringes the copyright holder's exclusive right to make reproductions of their works, or if it falls use
fair use
allowances.
[
28
]
[
29
]
United States
[
edit
]
U.S. machine learning developers have traditionally believed this to be allowable under fair use because using copyrighted work is
transformative
, and limited.
[
5
]
The situation has been compared to
Google Books
's scanning of copyrighted books in
Authors Guild, Inc. v. Google, Inc.
, which was ultimately found to be fair use, because the scanned content was not made publicly available, and the use was non-expressive.
[
30
]
Timothy B. Lee, in
Ars Technica
, argues that if the
plaintiffs
succeed, this may shift the balance of power in favour of large corporations such as Google, Microsoft, and Meta which can afford to license large amounts of training data from copyright holders and leverage their proprietary datasets of user-generated data.
[
30
]
IP
scholars Bryan Casey and
Mark Lemley
argue in the
Texas Law Review
that datasets are so large that "there is no plausible option simply to license all [of the data...]. So allowing [any generative training] copyright claim is tantamount to saying, not that copyright owners will get paid, but that the use won't be permitted at all."
[
31
]
Other scholars disagree; some predict a similar outcome to the U.S.
music licensing
procedures.
[
5
]
One of the earliest case to challenge the nature of fair use for training AI was a lawsuit that
Thomson Reuters
brought against Ross Intelligence first filed in 2020. Thomson Reuters argued that Ross Intelligence had used their
Westlaw
headnotes
, brief summaries of court decisions, to train their AI engine designed to compete with Westlaw. While Thomson Reuters' claims were initially denied by judge
Stephanos Bibas
of the
Third Circuit
on the basis that headnotes may not have been copyrightable, Bibas reevaluated his decision in February 2025 and issued a ruling favoring Thomson Reuters, in that headnotes are copyrightable, and that Ross Intelligence, which had since closed down in 2021, had inappropriately used the material. In the case of Ross's AI, the engine was not generative, and produced output that was composed of pieces of Westlaw's material, which aided in Thomson Reuter's claims of reuse, so how the case may apply to generative AI like OpenAI is not clear.
[
32
]
In a consolidated case brought by several authors against Meta and OpenAI, federal district judge
Vince Chhabria
expressed doubt that the use of unlicensed copyrighted material for training AI would fall under fair use. He stated during court hearings to Meta's lawyers that "You have companies using copyright-protected material to create a product that is capable of producing an infinite number of competing products. You are dramatically changing, you might even say obliterating, the market for that person's work, and you're saying that you don't even have to pay a license to that person. I just don't understand how that can be fair use."
[
33
]
Chhabria ruled a summary judgment in Meta's favor in June 2025, but based only on the lack of demonstration of sufficient harm of the output that Meta's LLM could produce, thus finding Meta's use of the authors' works fell within fair use. Chhabria emphasized his ruled did not mean that any use Meta made of copyrighted materials fell within fair use.
[
34
]
In a similar case, several authors including
Andrea Bartz
,
Charles Graeber
, and
Kirk Wallace Johnson
, sued
Anthropic
in August 2024, for using their works to train their AI model. Some of these works had been part of
the Pile
, intended as a collection of open source and public domain works but at times had included copyrighted works but since removed. Anthropic affirmed it has used the Pile but also had legally bought books and subsequently digitized them for training.
[
35
]
Judge
William Alsup
granted a summary judgment for Anthropic that affirmed that their use of purchased books for training was within fair use, but issues related to using the Pile with unlicensed works was not, and would face a separate trial related to damages.
[
36
]
Anthropic offered to settle on the latter matter in August 2025, preparing to pay the authors $1.5 billion, roughly $3000 for the 500,000 authors affected, and would have been the largest payout related to copyright infringement in the United States;
[
37
]
[
38
]
Alsup rejected the settlement over shortcomings in the settlement details that would be forced "down the throat of authors".
[
39
]
Alsup later retired in 2025, the case falling to Judge
Araceli Martinez-Olguin
who, by July 2026, approved of the original $1.5 billion settlement, overruling complaints from some affected authors that the settlement was too small.
[
40
]
The U.S. Copyright Office released a report that included review of public comment on matters of AI. Among other topics, the report addressed concerns about fair use of training materials, and considered that two of the fair use factors could be of concern. One factor was the purpose and character of the created work, where the Office directed to the Supreme Court decision in
Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, Inc. v. Goldsmith
that even though transformation had been performed, the works were still ultimately considered derivative works of the original copyright. The other factor was the impact on the commercial market, with the Office suggesting that AI models trained on copyrighted data to produce works in a specific style could have negative market impacts that would weaken the fair use defense.
[
41
]
EU
[
edit
]
In the EU, such text and data mining (TDM) exceptions form part of the 2019
Directive on Copyright in the Digital Single Market
.
[
42
]
They are specifically referred to in the EU's
AI Act
(which came into force in 2024), which "is widely seen as a clear indication of the EU legislator's intention that the exception covers AI data collection", a view that was also endorsed in a 2024 German court decision.
[
43
]
Unlike the TDM exception for scientific research, the more general exception covering commercial AI only applies if the copyright holder has not opted out.
[
43
]
In order to facilitate the opt-out to the TDM exception, the EU's AI Act of 2024 requires providers of "general-purpose" AI models to implement a policy to comply with EU law (including the TDM exception opt-out) and to publish a detailed summary of training content according to a template provided by the AI Office. These provisions will come into force in August 2025, with further clarification on exactly what will be required to providers of general-purpose AI models expected to come from a Code of Practice to be released in advance of this.
[
44
]
UK
[
edit
]
Unlike the EU, the United Kingdom prohibits data mining for commercial purposes but has proposed this should be changed to support the development of AI: "For text and data mining, we plan to introduce a new copyright and database exception which allows TDM for any purpose. Rights holders will still have safeguards to protect their content, including a requirement for lawful access."
[
24
]
India
[
edit
]
Indian copyright law provides fair use exceptions for scientific research, but lacks specific provisions for commercial AI training models. Unlike the EU and UK, India has not established TDM provisions that explicitly address commercial AI systems. This regulatory uncertainty became apparent in 2024 when
Asian News International
(ANI) sued OpenAI for using its content to train AI models without authorization. While OpenAI offered an opt-out policy that ANI used in October 2024 to block AI
scrapers
, ANI claimed this measure was ineffective since their content remained available through
content syndication
. The case also highlighted jurisdictional challenges, as OpenAI argued it was not subject to Indian law because its servers and training operations were located outside the country.
[
45
]
[
46
]
Copyright infringing AI outputs
[
edit
]
Generative AI models may produce outputs that are virtually identical to images from their training set.
The photograph on the left of
Anne Graham Lotz
was included in Stable Diffusion's training set; the image on the right was generated by Stable Diffusion using the prompt
Anne Graham Lotz
. The research paper from which this example was taken was able to produce similar replications for 0.03% of training images.
[
30
]
An image generated by
Flux
using the prompt
an astronaut riding a horse, by
Picasso
and
Juan Gris
. Generative image models are adept at imitating the visual style of particular artists in their training set.
In some cases, deep learning models may replicate items in their training set when generating output. This behaviour is generally considered an undesired
overfitting
of a model by AI developers, and has in previous generations of AI been considered a manageable problem.
[
47
]
Memorization
is the emergent phenomenon of LLMs to repeat long strings of training data, and it is no longer related to overfitting.
[
48
]
Evaluations of controlled LLM output measure the amount memorized from training data (focused on
GPT-2
-series models) as variously over 1% for exact duplicates
[
49
]
or up to about 7%.
[
50
]
This is potentially a security risk and a copyright risk, for both users and providers.
[
51
]
As of August 2023
[
update
]
, major consumer LLMs have attempted to mitigate these problems, but researchers have still been able to prompt leakage of copyrighted material.
[
52
]
Under U.S. law, to prove that an AI output infringes a copyright, a plaintiff must show the copyrighted work was "actually copied", meaning that the AI generates output which is "
substantially similar
" to their work, and that the AI had access to their work.
[
4
]
In the course of learning to statistically model the data on which they are trained, deep generative AI models may learn to imitate the distinct style of particular authors in the training set. Since
fictional characters enjoy some copyright protection
in the U.S. and other jurisdictions, an AI may also produce infringing content in the form of novel works which
incorporate fictional characters
.
[
4
]
[
30
]
A generative image model such as
Stable Diffusion
is able to model the stylistic characteristics of an artist like
Pablo Picasso
(including his particular brush strokes, use of colour, perspective, and so on), and a user can engineer a prompt such as "an astronaut riding a horse, by Picasso" to cause the model to generate a novel image applying the artist's style to an arbitrary subject. However, an artist's overall style is generally not subject to copyright protection.
[
4
]
Additional questions related to the copyrightability of style and the output of AI models was raised in March 2025, following an update to ChatGPT's model that was able to produce images strongly resembling the work of
Studio Ghibli
's artist
Hayao Miyazaki
. While users initially used it to make "Ghiblification" of popular meme images, further users were found to be distasteful in light of Miyazaki's negative stance on AI, and ChatGPT placed limits on the ability for users to make images in the style of living artists.
[
53
]
[
54
]
Litigation
[
edit
]
Doe v. GitHub, Inc.
[
edit
]
A
November 2022 class action
lawsuit against
Microsoft
,
GitHub
and
OpenAI
alleged that
GitHub Copilot
, an AI-powered code editing tool trained on public GitHub repositories, violated the copyright of the repositories' authors, noting that the tool was able to generate source code which matched its training data verbatim, without providing attribution.
[
55
]
Anderson v. Stability AI
[
edit
]
In January 2023 three US artists—
Sarah Andersen
,
Kelly McKernan
, and Karla Ortiz—filed a class action
copyright infringement
lawsuit against
Stability AI
,
Midjourney
, and
DeviantArt
, claiming that these companies have infringed the rights of millions of artists by training AI tools on five billion images scraped from the web without the consent of the original artists.
[
56
]
The plaintiffs' complaint has been criticized for technical inaccuracies, such as incorrectly claiming that "a trained diffusion model can produce a copy of any of its Training Images", and describing Stable Diffusion as "merely a complex collage tool".
[
57
]
In addition to copyright infringement, the plaintiffs allege unlawful competition and violation of their
right of publicity
in relation to AI tools' ability to create works in the style of the plaintiffs
en masse
.
[
57
]
In July 2023, U.S. District Judge
William Orrick
inclined to dismiss most of the lawsuit filed by Andersen, McKernan, and Ortiz but allowed them to file a new complaint.
[
58
]
Judge Orrick later dismissed all but one claim, that of copyright infringement towards Stability AI, in October 2023.
[
59
]
However, after refiling on some of the eliminated claims, Orrick agreed in August 2024 to include some of these additional claims against the AI companies, which included both copyright and trademark infringements.
[
60
]
Getty Images v. Stability AI
[
edit
]
In January 2023, Stability AI was sued in London by
Getty Images
for using its images in their training data without purchasing a license.
[
61
]
[
62
]
Getty filed another suit against
Stability AI
in a U.S. district court in Delaware in February 2023. The suit again alleges copyright infringement for the use of Getty's images in the training of Stable Diffusion, and further argues that the model infringes Getty's
trademark
by generating images with Getty's
watermark
.
[
63
]
Tremblay v. OpenAI, Inc.
[
edit
]
In July 2023, authors
Paul Tremblay
and
Mona Awad
filed a lawsuit in a San Francisco court against OpenAI, alleging that its ChatGPT language model had been trained on their copyrighted books without permission, citing ChatGPT's "very accurate" summaries of their works as evidence.
[
64
]
[
65
]
Two separate lawsuits were filed by authors
Sarah Silverman
,
Christopher Golden
and
Richard Kadrey
against Meta and OpenAI, arguing that in addition to copyright infringement for training their engines on their works, that products produced from the AI engines were derivative works and also copyright infringements.
[
66
]
The two suits against OpenAI were combined (during which Awad left the suit) and by February 2024, Judge
Araceli Martínez-Olguín
of the Northern District of California threw out all but one claim related to the use of the author's copyrighted works as part of the training data for the AI model.
[
67
]
Authors Guild et al v. OpenAI, Inc.
[
edit
]
The
Authors Guild
, on behalf of 17 authors, including
George R. R. Martin
, filed a copyright infringement complaint against OpenAI in September 2023, claiming "the company illegally copied the copyrighted works of authors" in training ChatGPT.
[
68
]
[
needs update
]
New York Times v. Microsoft and OpenAI
[
edit
]
In December 2023,
The New York Times
sued
Microsoft
and
OpenAI
.
The New York Times
is a global media company that publishes content in print and online forms, generating revenue from subscriptions, advertising, and licensing.
[
69
]
The
Times
claimed that ChatGPT and Bing's AI models were trained on articles from the Times and provided end-users with responses based on these works,
[
70
]
which the
Times
considers infringement of their copyright. The
Times
further claimed that fair use claims made by these AI companies were invalid since the generated information around news stories directly competes with the
Times
and impacts the newspaper's commercial opportunities.
[
71
]
Moreover, the plaintiffs contended that the hallucinations created by LLMs were damaging the reputation of the
Times.
[
70
]
In March 2025, the federal district judge denied Microsoft and OpenAI's motion to dismiss the lawsuit, while narrowing the
Times
' claims to those related to copyright infringement in training OpenAI's models.
[
72
]
The court held that Microsoft and OpenAI can be held liable for direct copyright infringement, contributory copyright infringement, and state and federal trademark dilution claims. However, claims based on common law unfair competition are not plausible, and therefore Microsoft and OpenAI cannot be held liable.
[
73
]
Daily News LP v. Microsoft Corp.
[
edit
]
Eight U.S. national newspapers owned by
Tribune Publishing
sued Microsoft and OpenAI in April 2024 over copyright infringement related to the use of their news articles for training data, as well as for output that creates false and misleading statements that are attributed to the newspapers.
[
74
]
UMG Recordings, Inc. et al v. Suno, Inc. et al
[
edit
]
The
Recording Industry Association of America
(RIAA) and several major music labels sued the developers of
Suno AI
and
Udio
, AI models that can take text input to create songs with both lyrics and backing music, in separate lawsuits in June 2024, alleging that both AI models were trained without consent with music from the labels.
[
75
]
[
76
]
Robert Kneschke v. LAION
[
edit
]
In September 2024, the
Regional Court of Hamburg
dismissed a German photographer's lawsuit against the non-profit organization
LAION
for unauthorized reproduction of his copyrighted work while creating a dataset for AI training.
[
42
]
The decision was described as a "landmark ruling on TDM exceptions for AI training data" in Germany and EU more generally.
[
42
]
The plaintiff has filed an appeal against the decision.

Title: Copyrightability of AI Generated Work: Legal Challenges & Guidance
Content: , and the implications of joint ownership of AI models and output.
AI-generated works must meet the human authorship requirement to be eligible for copyright protection according to the U.S. Copyright Office, which has refused registration for AI-generated images due to the unpredictability of the output and the lack of sufficient human authorship. Different countries, however, have varying approaches to copyright protection for AI-generated works, which our speakers discuss. Take this course for insights into specific cases that illustrate the challenge of determining human authorship in AI-generated works, guidance and disclosure rules established by the Copyright Office, the importance of addressing copyright ownership and usage rights in AI-related license agreements, recent cases, and the implications of joint ownership of AI models and output.

Title: Copyright Protection for AI-Generated Works (BitLaw)
Content: The approach to this issue by the Patent Office appears to be a more practical solution for handling joint human/AI activity. The problem with the Copyright Office's current approach is that AI-assisted creative content is rarely produced in a way that allows for clear separation of human and machine contributions. The process of generating AI-assisted works—whether texts, images, or other media—typically involves hundreds of iterative interactions between human creators and AI tools, making it nearly impossible to pinpoint discrete portions that are wholly human-created. This challenge is especially pressing in fields like literature, photography, filmmaking, and music, where AI is becoming an essential creative tool. If the Copyright Office maintains its stance, many of these works will remain unprotected because the requirement for separable human authorship renders them ineligible. # Legal Implications of AI-Generated Content and Copyright Law

The intersection of artificial intelligence (AI) and copyright law has become a focal point of legal discourse as AI technologies advance and proliferate across various creative industries. This report explores the legal implications of AI-generated content, focusing on copyrightability, ownership, and the evolving landscape of litigation surrounding these issues. 

## The Human Authorship Requirement

### Current Legal Framework

Under U.S. copyright law, a fundamental principle is that only works created by human authors can receive copyright protection. The U.S. Copyright Office has consistently maintained that AI-generated works, which lack human authorship, are ineligible for copyright. This stance was reaffirmed in the 2025 Copyrightability Report, which stated that authorship must involve human intellectual input and expressive choice, which AI systems do not possess ([BitLaw](https://www.bitlaw.com/ai/AI-copyright.html)). 

In practical terms, this means that if an AI system generates content independently, without meaningful human input, the resulting work is not eligible for copyright protection. Conversely, if a human contributor significantly shapes, arranges, or modifies AI-generated material in a way that reflects original human authorship, copyright protection may be granted for those specific human contributions ([BitLaw](https://www.bitlaw.com/ai/AI-copyright.html)).

### The Challenge of Separability

A significant challenge in determining copyright eligibility for AI-assisted works is the ability to separate human-created elements from AI-generated content. The Copyright Office has emphasized that if AI-generated enhancements are so integrated that the original human authorship can no longer be identified as distinct from the machine-generated content, the work as a whole will not qualify for copyright protection ([BitLaw](https://www.bitlaw.com/ai/AI-copyright.html)). 

For example, in the case of Sahni, an applicant who attempted to register an AI-generated image, the court found that the AI's transformation was so pervasive that the human contribution was no longer distinguishable, rendering the work uncopyrightable ([BitLaw](https://www.bitlaw.com/ai/AI-copyright.html)). This "separability" requirement poses a significant barrier for creators utilizing AI tools, as many creative processes involve iterative interactions between human creators and AI systems.

## International Perspectives on Copyright for AI-Generated Works

### Varied Approaches

Different countries have adopted varying approaches to copyright protection for AI-generated works. For instance, while the U.S. maintains a strict human authorship requirement, other jurisdictions are exploring more flexible frameworks. In November 2023, the Beijing Internet Court recognized copyright in AI-generated images, suggesting a more permissive stance towards AI-generated content ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence_and_copyright)).

The European Union is also developing legislation that seeks to balance innovation with intellectual property protection. The EU's 2019 Directive on Copyright introduced specific exceptions allowing text and data mining of works for AI research while permitting rightsholders to opt out of commercial AI mining ([New York State Bar Association](https://nysba.org/copyright-law-in-the-age-of-ai-navigating-authorship-infringement-and-creative-rights)). This indicates a growing recognition of the need to adapt copyright frameworks to accommodate the realities of AI technologies.

### Implications for Global Trade

The divergence in international copyright approaches raises concerns regarding global trade and the potential for regulatory discrepancies. Companies operating across borders may face challenges in navigating these varied legal landscapes, which could impact their ability to leverage AI technologies effectively. 

## Copyright Ownership and Usage Rights

### Joint Ownership Issues

The question of ownership becomes particularly complex in cases involving AI-generated content. The U.S. Copyright Office has firmly rejected the notion that humans and AI can work together as joint authors, clarifying that authorship must involve human intellectual input ([BitLaw](https://www.bitlaw.com/ai/AI-copyright.html)). This rejection of joint authorship principles raises significant concerns for creators who rely on AI as a collaborative tool.

In contrast, the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office has adopted a more pragmatic approach, utilizing the concept of co-inventors to determine when AI-assisted inventions are protected by patent laws ([BitLaw](https://www.bitlaw.com/ai/AI-copyright.html)). This distinction highlights the differing treatment of AI in copyright versus patent law and underscores the need for a cohesive legal framework that addresses the unique challenges posed by AI technologies.

### Licensing Agreements

As the legal landscape surrounding AI-generated content continues to evolve, the importance of addressing copyright ownership and usage rights in AI-related license agreements cannot be overstated. Companies may benefit from implementing formal licensing arrangements to clarify rights and responsibilities concerning the use of copyrighted materials in AI training and outputs. Such agreements could mitigate litigation risks and provide clearer pathways for utilizing AI technologies while respecting intellectual property rights ([Norton Rose Fulbright](https://www.nortonrosefulbright.com/en/knowledge/publications/ce8eaa5f/ai-in-litigation-series-an-update-on-ai-copyright-cases-in-2026)).

## Litigation Trends and Legal Challenges

### Ongoing Lawsuits

The rapid advancement of AI technologies has led to a surge in litigation related to copyright infringement and ownership of AI-generated content. High-profile cases, such as *Thaler v. Perlmutter* and *Getty Images v. Stability AI*, illustrate the complexities surrounding the use of copyrighted materials to train AI models and the ownership of AI-generated outputs ([Norton Rose Fulbright](https://www.nortonrosefulbright.com/en/knowledge/publications/ce8eaa5f/ai-in-litigation-series-an-update-on-ai-copyright-cases-in-2026)). 

These cases raise fundamental questions about whether training AI on copyrighted works constitutes fair use and whether AI-generated outputs infringe copyrights or are copyrightable. The evolving nature of these legal challenges underscores the need for courts to refine the application of copyright law to address the unique characteristics of AI technologies.

### Fair Use Doctrine

The fair use doctrine plays a critical role in the ongoing legal debates surrounding AI-generated content. Courts are grappling with whether the use of copyrighted works to train AI models falls under fair use, which involves a four-factor test analyzing the purpose and character of the use, the nature of the copyrighted work, the amount and substantiality of the portion used, and the effect of the use on the potential market ([Norton Rose Fulbright](https://www.nortonrosefulbright.com/en/knowledge/publications/ce8eaa5f/ai-in-litigation-series-an-update-on-ai-copyright-cases-in-2026)). 

The outcomes of these cases will likely shape the legal landscape for AI technologies and influence how companies approach the use of copyrighted materials in their AI models.

## Conclusion

The legal implications of AI-generated content and copyright law present a complex and evolving landscape. While the U.S. maintains a strict human authorship requirement, international perspectives are beginning to explore more flexible frameworks for copyright protection. The challenges of separability, ownership, and usage rights highlight the need for a cohesive legal framework that addresses the unique characteristics of AI technologies. 

As litigation surrounding AI-generated content continues to unfold, it is imperative for creators, technology companies, and legal practitioners to stay informed about the evolving legal landscape and to consider proactive measures, such as licensing agreements, to navigate the complexities of copyright law in the age of AI.
